**The Monthly Mailbag With Campbell Rawlins**
**August 30, 2026**
At the beginning of every month, a different Dispatch staffer fields questions from members and compiles his or her answers in a mailbag a few weeks later. This month, it was Campbell Rawlins’ turn.

**Question from Howmanydiscs:**
*How long did it take you to become a “good” home cook? I’m cooking three nights a week for my family now, but I’m slow, prone to major oversights, and don’t feel like I’m getting much better. Is the answer to just hand the reins back to my wife?*
It feels a little self-important to declare yourself a “good cook,” but I do think I’ve become a pretty solid one. Honestly, it took a lot of time in the kitchen and experimentation. I worked in restaurants through college and graduate school and became obsessed with food along the way. I was always an adventurous eater, but working in restaurants taught me to pay attention to why things tasted good together. At one high-end restaurant in Boston, we servers were quizzed on every ingredient in every dish.

Eventually, you start to understand that certain cuisines have a grammar to them. The same flavors and ingredients show up in different combinations repeatedly. When I started cooking for myself, I tried to learn that grammar rather than just learn recipes. My advice: Don’t worry so much about executing increasingly complicated recipes perfectly. Understanding why ingredients work together teaches you how to cook. You’ll eventually stop needing the recipe because you understand what you’re trying to make.

One cookbook that helped me is Sam Kass’ *Eat a Little Better*. Many recipes are intentionally simple and designed to be adapted. They give you a foundation and encourage you to play around. That’s the key—learn a handful of things you can riff on rather than 50 recipes to follow strictly. Cooking became much more fun for me once it felt like experimenting rather than completing an assignment. So absolutely do not hand the reins back to your wife!

**Question from cassi123:**
*Recommend a fun weeknight recipe that doesn’t take 90 minutes (which is what usually happens to me!).*
Jamaican jerk chicken bowls. I went to Jamaica a couple of years ago for a friend’s wedding, where each guest house had its own chef. I spent a lot of time talking to ours about how she cooked, and I came home with a bunch of Jamaican spices and ideas. This dish has become one of our go-to dinners.

The basic formula is jerk-seasoned chicken thighs, coconut rice, and a salsa of equal parts avocado and mango with cilantro, green onions, lime, cumin, and coriander. Top it with cotija, pickled red onions, and another squeeze of lime. I swear by Easispice jerk seasoning—the real Jamaican stuff—and don’t be shy with it. I usually smoke the chicken and then char it on the grill, but grilling the thighs is almost as good and makes the whole thing painless. Make extra chicken and salsa and you’ve also solved lunch for the next day.

**Question from H.W.:**
*As someone who also “spends an unreasonable amount of time thinking about music,” what are some of your favorite artists or albums? Any new music recommendations? Anyone I’ve probably never heard of but should listen to?*
Obsessively. I came of age during the Napster era and at one point had a carefully maintained library of more than 20,000 songs. Streaming was an uncomfortable adjustment because suddenly the collection wasn’t really mine anymore. Playlists became my way of hanging onto the mixtape part of music listening. I have hundreds on Spotify. I make one every season where I dump new music I’m discovering, plus longer-running playlists for particular moods. My current favorite is called *Chilled Red*: humid summer evening, bottle of chilled red wine, something on the grill, friends hanging around longer than planned.

A few things I’ve been listening to lately: Ovven, which reminds me of MJ Lenderman or Greg Freeman; Cece Coakley, if you like Waxahatchee, Lucinda Williams, or Sierra Ferrell; La Reezy, a fantastic New Orleans rapper; the new Phoebe Bridgers record; and the new Weezer album, produced by Kenny Beats, which manages to feel both nostalgic and modern.
